resources.name: Golden Dataset Construction
resources.description: Builds versioned evaluation datasets for LLM features: coverage matrix, sourcing from logs and synthesis, edge and adversarial cases, reference labeling, contamination checks, and dataset versioning.
resources.purpose: Evals are only as good as the cases they contain. Ad-hoc test sets over-represent easy happy paths, leak into prompts, and silently change between runs. This skill gives a structured method to define coverage, source and label cases, record provenance, split dev from held-out sets, and version the dataset so results stay comparable over time.

safety.notes: Production logs used as eval cases may contain personal or confidential data; requires de-identification and consent review before inclusion. Never stores secrets in the dataset.

files.content:
---
name: golden-dataset-construction
description: Build a versioned golden evaluation dataset for an LLM feature - coverage matrix, sourcing from production logs and targeted synthesis, edge and adversarial cases, reference labels, provenance, dev/held-out splits, and contamination checks. Use when starting evals for a feature, when existing test sets feel unrepresentative, or before comparing models or prompts.
---

# Golden Dataset Construction

## When to use
- Starting an evaluation suite for a new LLM feature.
- Existing eval cases are mostly happy paths, were written by one person, or no longer match traffic.
- Preparing a fixed benchmark before a model upgrade or a prompt optimization effort.

Not for: writing the scoring method (see `llm-judge-rubric-design`) or detailed annotator instructions (see `data-labeling-guidelines`). Generating individual cases from a prompt is covered by `eval-test-case-generator-prompt`; this skill governs the dataset as a whole.

## Inputs
- Feature spec: inputs, expected behaviour, policies, and what must never happen.
- Access to de-identified production samples, support tickets, or user research, if they exist.
- Known failure reports and bug tickets.
- Who can provide authoritative reference answers (domain experts, policy owners).

## Procedure
1. **Define the coverage matrix.** List the dimensions that change behaviour: intent or task type, input length, language, user segment, difficulty, and required behaviour (answer, ask clarifying question, refuse, escalate). The matrix rows are the cells you must populate; mark cells that are rare in traffic but high in risk.
2. **Source cases in layers.**
   - Real traffic sample (stratified, de-identified) for representativeness.
   - Failure-driven cases from bug reports and support escalations.
   - Targeted synthetic cases for empty cells: edge inputs (empty, very long, mixed language, malformed), ambiguous requests, out-of-scope requests, and adversarial inputs relevant to the feature.
   Tag every case with its source; synthetic cases should be reviewed by a person before inclusion.
3. **Size by purpose, not by habit.** A smoke set of 20-50 cases catches breakage quickly. Decision-grade comparisons usually need a few hundred cases so per-segment results are not dominated by noise. Aim for at least about 20-30 cases in any segment you intend to report separately; treat this as a rule of thumb.
4. **Write reference labels.** Depending on the task: exact answers, acceptable answer sets, required facts that must appear, forbidden content, or the correct behaviour class. Prefer "must include / must not include" checklists over a single gold paragraph for open-ended tasks. Have a second person review a sample of references; log disagreements and resolve them.
5. **Record schema and provenance.** Each case: `id`, `input` (and conversation history or retrieved context if fixed), `expected` (reference or checklist), `behaviour_class`, `tags`, `source`, `difficulty`, `created_by`, `reviewed_by`, `added_in_version`, `notes`.
6. **Split.** Keep a dev split for iteration and a held-out split that is used only for final decisions. Never copy held-out cases into prompts as few-shot examples.
7. **Check for contamination and duplication.** Remove near-duplicates (normalize and compare text, or embed and threshold similarity). Search prompts and few-shot banks for overlap with the held-out set. If public benchmark items are used, note the risk that models saw them in training.
8. **Version and govern.** Store as JSONL or CSV in version control with a changelog. Bump the version on any change; never edit a case silently, deprecate it and add a new one. Record the version with every eval result.
9. **Refresh on a schedule.** Each cycle, add cases from new failures and traffic drift, and retire cases whose expected behaviour changed due to policy updates.

## Expected output
```markdown
## Golden dataset: <feature> v<x.y>
Cases: <total> (dev <n>, held-out <m>) | sources: traffic <a>%, failures <b>%, synthetic <c>%
| Coverage cell | Cases | Risk | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Refund request, non-English | 24 | high | |

Case schema: id, input, expected, behaviour_class, tags, source, difficulty, created_by, reviewed_by, added_in_version
Reference review: <n> double-reviewed, agreement <x>%
Dedup/contamination checks: <method, removed count>
Changelog: v<x.y> - added 40 cases from Q3 escalations; deprecated 6 cases after policy change
```

## Constraints and limitations
- Production data must be de-identified and used under applicable consent and retention rules before it enters a dataset.
- Synthetic cases reflect the generator's blind spots; cap their share and keep them labeled.
- A dataset tuned against repeatedly loses its value as a held-out measure; rotate held-out cases periodically.
- Do not state that a dataset is "representative" without showing the traffic sample it was compared against.

## Examples
A contract-summary feature had 60 eval cases, all short English NDAs. The coverage matrix exposed missing cells for long master agreements, scanned PDFs with OCR noise, and non-English contracts. Adding 120 cases across those cells, with clause-level must-include checklists reviewed by a lawyer, revealed that the "95% pass rate" fell to 71% on long agreements, which redirected work to chunked summarization.

resources.purpose: GraphQL schemas are long-lived contracts queried in shapes the server does not control. This skill reviews schema design and resolver behaviour together, catching nullability that blanks whole responses, unbounded lists, per-row resolver queries, and breaking changes before clients depend on them.

safety.notes: Review only; breaking-change classifications should be confirmed against real client usage before removal.

files.content:
---
name: graphql-schema-review
description: Reviews a GraphQL schema (SDL) and its resolvers for nullability design, Relay-style connection pagination, input and mutation payload conventions, N+1 resolver patterns and DataLoader batching, query cost limits, and safe evolution via @deprecated. Use when designing a new GraphQL API, reviewing a schema change, or diagnosing slow or fragile GraphQL endpoints.
---

# GraphQL Schema Review

A GraphQL schema is a long-lived public contract that clients query in shapes you do not control. Mistakes in nullability, pagination, and mutation design are expensive to undo, and naive resolvers turn one query into hundreds of database calls. This skill reviews the schema and the resolver layer together.

## When to use

- Designing or reviewing a GraphQL schema or a schema change (SDL diff).
- A GraphQL endpoint is slow, and per-field resolvers are suspected.
- Planning deprecations or federation/subgraph boundaries.

Not for: OpenAPI/REST contracts (`openapi-spec-authoring`), or a cross-protocol API design assessment (`api-design-review-agent`).

## Inputs

- The schema SDL (or introspection result) and, for a change, the diff against production.
- Resolver code for the types under review, and the data-access layer they call.
- Client usage if available: persisted queries, operation logs, field usage from a schema registry.
- Server stack (Apollo Server, GraphQL Yoga, graphql-java, Hot Chocolate, gqlgen, Strawberry) — features differ.

## Procedure

1. **Check naming and shape.** Types in PascalCase, fields and arguments in camelCase, enums values in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE. Model the domain, not the database: no `user_id: Int` foreign keys where a `user: User` field belongs. Use custom scalars for meaningful formats (`DateTime`, `URL`, `Email`) with documented serialisation. Every type and non-obvious field has a description.

2. **Review nullability deliberately.** In GraphQL, a resolver error on a non-null field nulls out the nearest nullable parent, so over-using `!` makes one failing field blank an entire response. Guidelines (heuristics, choose per field): IDs and fields that cannot fail independently can be non-null; fields backed by separate services or that may be hidden by authorisation should usually be nullable; lists are typically `[Item!]!` (list always present, no null entries). Arguments: non-null when required. Changing nullable to non-null on an output field is safe for clients; the reverse is breaking — and for inputs the rules invert.

3. **Check pagination.** Unbounded lists (`orders: [Order!]!` on a customer with thousands of orders) are a performance and availability risk. Use the Relay Cursor Connections pattern for growing collections: `orders(first: Int, after: String, last: Int, before: String): OrderConnection!` with `edges { cursor node }`, `pageInfo { hasNextPage hasPreviousPage startCursor endCursor }`, and optionally `nodes` and `totalCount` (only if it is cheap to compute). Enforce a maximum `first`. Cursors should be opaque.

4. **Review mutations.** One mutation per user intent (`cancelOrder`, not `updateOrder(status: CANCELLED)` for everything). Single `input` argument of a dedicated input type (`CancelOrderInput!`), and a dedicated payload type (`CancelOrderPayload`) returning the changed object plus expected, user-facing errors as data (e.g. a `userErrors: [UserError!]!` field or a result union `CancelOrderResult = CancelOrderSuccess | OrderNotCancellable`). Reserve top-level `errors` for unexpected failures. Support idempotency for retried mutations where duplicates matter (client-supplied id or key).

5. **Find N+1 resolver patterns.** A field resolver that queries per parent (`Order.customer` doing `SELECT ... WHERE id = ?` for each of 50 orders) is the classic problem. Fix with DataLoader-style batching and per-request caching: collect keys during one tick, load with `WHERE id = ANY($keys)`, return results in key order (with nulls or errors for missing keys). Create loaders per request to avoid leaking data across users. Check list fields nested inside list fields for multiplicative cost.

6. **Check abuse protection.** Depth limiting, query cost or complexity analysis (assign costs per field and multiply by requested page size), maximum page sizes, timeouts, and — for first-party clients — persisted queries or an operation allow-list. Consider disabling introspection in production only if the API is private; it is not a security boundary on its own.

7. **Check authorisation placement.** Authorisation belongs in the business/data layer or a consistent field-level mechanism, not only on top-level query fields: nested paths (`order { customer { paymentMethods } }`) bypass checks placed only at the root.

8. **Review evolution.** Prefer additive change. Use `@deprecated(reason: "Use fulfilment.status. Removal after 2027-03-01.")` on fields and enum values (and input fields/arguments where the server supports the newer spec), track usage, and remove only when usage reaches zero. Run a schema diff tool (GraphQL Inspector, Apollo `rover graph check`) to classify breaking vs dangerous vs safe changes; adding an enum value is "dangerous" because exhaustive client switches may break.

## Expected output

```markdown
### Scope
<schema version/diff, resolvers reviewed>
### Findings
| # | Severity | Area | Location (Type.field) | Issue | Recommendation |
Areas: naming, nullability, pagination, mutation design, N+1, cost limits, authz, evolution
### Proposed SDL changes
    <SDL>
### Resolver changes
<DataLoader sketch, batched query>
### Breaking-change report
| Change | Classification | Client impact | Mitigation |
```

## Constraints and limitations

- Server and library behaviour (deprecation on input fields, `@oneOf` input support, defer/stream) varies by implementation and spec version; verify against the stack in use.
- Do not label a change safe without checking client usage when a registry or operation logs exist.
- Nullability choices are trade-offs; present the reasoning rather than a blanket rule.
- Performance claims need measurement (resolver tracing, query count per operation).

## Examples

**Schema excerpt:** `type Customer { orders: [Order]! }`, with `Order.items` and `Item.product` each resolved by a per-row SQL query.
**Findings:** unbounded list — replace with `orders(first: Int = 20, after: String): OrderConnection!` capped at 100 (major); nullable list entries `[Order]` should be `[Order!]` unless partial failure is intended (minor); a request for 20 orders with 5 items each issues 1 + 20 + 100 queries — batch `Order.items` and `Item.product` with per-request DataLoaders to make it 3 queries (major, measured by the user with query logging).

resources.name: Hallucination Detection
resources.description: Detects unsupported content in LLM outputs by extracting atomic claims, matching each to source evidence, and labeling it supported, contradicted, or unverifiable, with aggregate faithfulness metrics.
resources.purpose: Fluent answers can contain fabricated numbers, citations, and entities that reviewers miss. This skill breaks an output into checkable atomic claims, verifies each against the provided sources or a trusted reference, and reports which claims fail and why, giving both a per-answer audit and a faithfulness rate that can be tracked over time.

safety.notes: Verifies only against sources the user supplies or explicitly authorizes; never presents its own unsourced knowledge as verification. Not a substitute for expert review in medical, legal, or financial content.

files.content:
---
name: hallucination-detection
description: Detect unsupported or fabricated content in LLM outputs by decomposing the output into atomic claims, retrieving or locating evidence for each in the supplied sources, labeling each claim supported, contradicted, or not verifiable, and reporting per-answer findings plus faithfulness rates. Use for auditing RAG answers, summaries, reports, and citations before they reach users or as an evaluation metric.
---

# Hallucination Detection

## When to use
- Auditing a RAG answer, summary, or generated report against its source documents.
- Checking that citations actually support the sentences they are attached to.
- Building a faithfulness metric for an evaluation suite or production sampling.

Not for: judging style or helpfulness (see `llm-judge-rubric-design`) or measuring whether the retriever found the right documents (see `retrieval-quality-metrics`). This skill checks the output against evidence; it is not open-ended fact-checking against the whole web.

## Inputs
- The output to check.
- The evidence set: retrieved passages, source documents, or a trusted reference. For closed-book outputs, the user must name an authoritative reference; without one, claims can only be marked not verifiable.
- The definition of "supported" for this use (strict entailment, or allowed paraphrase and common knowledge).

## Procedure
1. **Fix the standard of support.** Decide up front: is general background knowledge allowed, or must every factual claim be grounded in the sources? For RAG features grounded-only is usually the right standard. Write the rule down so labels are consistent.
2. **Extract atomic claims.** Split the output into the smallest independently checkable statements. "Acme was founded in 2009 in Berlin by two engineers" becomes three claims. Resolve pronouns so each claim stands alone. Skip non-factual content (greetings, hedges, opinions marked as such) but keep implicit claims, such as a recommendation that presupposes a fact.
3. **Locate evidence for each claim.** Search the evidence set for the passage(s) that bear on the claim. Quote the exact span. If the output cites a source, check the cited source first, then the others.
4. **Label each claim.**
   - Supported: the evidence entails the claim.
   - Contradicted: the evidence states something incompatible.
   - Not verifiable: no evidence either way (this is a hallucination under a grounded-only standard).
   - Partially supported: some elements match, others do not; record which element fails.
   Pay special attention to high-risk categories: numbers, dates, names, quotations, citations, causal claims, and negations.
5. **Check citations separately.** For each citation, record whether the cited passage supports the sentence it is attached to. A true claim attached to the wrong source is a citation error, not a factual one, and needs a different fix.
6. **Aggregate.** Faithfulness = supported claims / checkable claims. Also report the share of answers with at least one contradicted or unverifiable claim, since users experience answers, not claims. Break down by claim type.
7. **Automate carefully.** An LLM can perform steps 2-4 with a natural-language-inference style prompt per claim (premise = evidence span, hypothesis = claim). Calibrate it on a human-labeled sample of claims before trusting its rates, and keep a human review sample in production.
8. **Feed fixes back.** Map findings to causes: retrieval missed the evidence, the generator ignored it, the prompt allowed background knowledge, or the source itself was wrong.

## Expected output
```markdown
## Hallucination audit: <output id>
Standard: <grounded-only | background allowed>
| # | Claim | Label | Evidence (quote, source) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Plan includes 5 seats | Contradicted | "The Team plan includes 3 seats" (pricing.md) | number error |
| 2 | Annual billing gets a discount | Not verifiable | none found | |

Citation check: 4/5 citations support their sentence
Faithfulness: 7/9 checkable claims supported (0.78)
Likely cause: generator added background knowledge; retrieval did contain the correct seat count
```

## Constraints and limitations
- Never mark a claim supported from your own knowledge when the standard is grounded-only; mark it not verifiable.
- Claim extraction is itself error-prone; inconsistent granularity skews rates, so keep extraction rules fixed across comparisons.
- Sources can be wrong or outdated; a supported claim is faithful to the source, not necessarily true.
- For medical, legal, or financial content, automated checks support but do not replace expert review.

## Examples
A policy assistant answered a parental-leave question with six claims. Five matched the HR policy; one ("leave can be split into three blocks") was not verifiable, since the policy only mentioned two blocks. The retrieved context contained the correct rule, so the fix targeted the generation prompt (forbid adding unstated conditions) rather than retrieval.

resources.name: Hybrid Search Tuning
resources.description: Tunes hybrid lexical plus vector retrieval: BM25 configuration, fusion with reciprocal rank fusion or weighted scores, candidate depth, cross-encoder reranking, and weight sweeps measured on a labeled query set.
resources.purpose: Pure vector search misses exact identifiers and rare terms, while pure BM25 misses paraphrase. Hybrid retrieval fixes both only when fusion, candidate depth, and reranking are tuned on real queries. This skill gives a measured procedure for choosing a fusion method and parameters, adding reranking where it pays off, and checking latency, so hybrid search improves recall without guesswork.

safety.notes: Operates on the user's own index and query logs; recommends anonymizing logged queries before labeling. No network access required.

files.content:
---
name: hybrid-search-tuning
description: Tune hybrid retrieval that combines BM25 lexical search with vector search - analyzer and BM25 settings, fusion via reciprocal rank fusion or normalized weighted scores, candidate depth, cross-encoder reranking, and parameter sweeps measured on labeled queries with latency checks. Use when vector-only or keyword-only search misses relevant results, or when an existing hybrid setup uses untuned defaults.
---

# Hybrid Search Tuning

## When to use
- Vector search misses exact identifiers, product codes, error messages, names, or rare terms.
- Keyword search misses paraphrases and conceptual queries.
- A hybrid setup exists but its fusion weights or reranker were never measured.

Not for: deciding chunk boundaries (see `chunking-strategy-design`) or choosing a vector database (see `vector-database-evaluation-agent`). This skill depends on `retrieval-quality-metrics` for measurement.

## Inputs
- A labeled query set with relevance judgments, ideally 100+ queries, tagged by query type (identifier lookup, keyword, natural-language question, conceptual).
- Access to both retrievers' ranked results with scores, and to a reranker if one is available.
- Latency budget for the retrieval stage and the final k sent to the generator.

## Procedure
1. **Baseline each retriever alone.** Compute recall@k and MRR or nDCG for BM25-only and vector-only, per query type. Typical pattern: BM25 wins on identifiers and rare terms, vectors win on paraphrase. If one retriever dominates every segment, hybrid may add latency without benefit.
2. **Fix the lexical side first.** Check analyzers: tokenization of codes and hyphenated ids, stemming, stop words, and language handling. Field boosts (title over body) often matter more than BM25 parameters. BM25's k1 (term-frequency saturation, commonly around 1.2) and b (length normalization, commonly 0.75) are reasonable defaults; tune them only after analyzer issues are fixed, and only on the labeled set.
3. **Choose a fusion method.**
   - Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF): score(d) = sum over retrievers of 1 / (k + rank(d)), with k commonly set to 60. It uses ranks only, so it needs no score normalization and is a robust default.
   - Weighted score fusion: score = alpha x norm(vector) + (1 - alpha) x norm(bm25), with min-max or z-score normalization per query. It can outperform RRF when tuned, but it is sensitive to score distributions that shift across queries and index updates.
   Start with RRF; try weighted fusion if per-segment results suggest one retriever should count more.
4. **Set candidate depth.** Retrieve N candidates from each retriever before fusion (for example 50-100 each), so that relevant documents ranked moderately by one retriever can still surface. Measure recall@N of the union; if it is low, no fusion or reranking can recover the missing documents.
5. **Sweep parameters.** Grid over RRF k (for example 10, 30, 60, 100) and per-retriever weights, or alpha in steps of 0.1 for weighted fusion. Evaluate on a tuning split and confirm the chosen setting on a held-out split. Report per-segment results, not just the mean.
6. **Add reranking if it pays.** A cross-encoder reranker scores each query-candidate pair jointly and usually improves top-k precision. Rerank the top M fused candidates (for example 20-100). Measure gain in recall@k and nDCG at the generator's k against added latency and cost; choose M at the knee of that curve.
7. **Apply filters correctly.** Metadata and permission filters must apply to both retrievers before fusion, otherwise one side can leak or crowd out filtered results.
8. **Check latency end to end.** Run both retrievers in parallel; measure p50 and p95 for retrieval, fusion, and reranking separately.
9. **Record the configuration** with the query set and qrels versions, and re-run the evaluation when the embedding model, analyzer, or corpus changes materially.

## Expected output
```markdown
## Hybrid search tuning: <index> (queries v<x>, qrels v<y>)
| Config | Recall@5 | nDCG@10 | Identifier recall@5 | Question recall@5 | p95 latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BM25 only | | | | | |
| Vector only | | | | | |
| RRF k=60, N=100 | | | | | |
| RRF + rerank top 50 | | | | | |
Union recall@N: <x>
Chosen config: <fusion, params, N, M>; held-out confirmation: <metric values>
Trade-offs and follow-ups: ...
```

## Constraints and limitations
- Parameter values quoted above are common starting points, not universal optima; the labeled set decides.
- Tuning on few queries overfits; keep a held-out split and report segments with their sizes.
- Reranker gains depend on domain match; a general reranker may underperform on specialized jargon.
- Score-based fusion must be re-checked after re-indexing or model changes because score scales shift.

## Examples
An internal IT knowledge base used vector-only search; queries containing error codes like `0x80070005` had recall@5 of 0.31. Adding BM25 with an analyzer that kept hex codes intact and fusing with RRF (k=60, 50 candidates each) raised error-code recall@5 to 0.84 while question-style queries stayed flat. A reranker over the top 30 added a further gain on questions at an acceptable p95 latency, so both were adopted.

# Incident Postmortem Routine

## Objective
Turn a resolved incident into durable learning: an accurate timeline, a clear statement of impact, an analysis of the contributing factors that made the incident possible and slowed recovery, and a small set of owned, verifiable action items that are tracked to completion. The review is blameless: it assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew and the tools they had, and it looks for the system conditions that allowed the failure. Diagnosis during the incident itself belongs to `production-incident-debugger-agent`; this routine starts once service is restored.

## Trigger
Run it after any incident that meets your organisation's postmortem criteria. If none exist, a reasonable starting heuristic is: any customer-visible outage or data issue, any breach of an SLO error budget threshold, any security event, any incident needing a rollback of a release, or a near miss that would have been serious. Start the draft within two working days while memory is fresh, and hold the review meeting within about a week. The routine is a facilitation guide for people; it does not run itself.

## Prerequisites
- Service restored and the incident formally closed or downgraded.
- A named facilitator who was not the primary responder, if possible, to keep the discussion neutral.
- Access to the incident channel history, alerts, dashboards, deploy logs, tickets and any customer reports.
- Agreement from leadership that the review is blameless and that findings will not be used for individual performance evaluation.

## Inputs
- Required: incident channel or call notes, alert and paging history, deploy and config change logs for the window, metrics and logs around detection and recovery.
- Optional: customer support tickets, status page updates, previous postmortems for the same service, runbooks used, on-call handover notes.

## Steps
1. **Collect evidence before opinions.** Export the incident channel, alerts, graphs and change logs into the draft. Note gaps in evidence (missing logs, unrecorded manual actions) as findings in their own right.
2. **Build the timeline.** In UTC, list events from the triggering change or condition through detection, escalation, diagnosis, mitigation and full recovery. Each entry: timestamp, what happened, source of evidence. Mark the key intervals: time to detect, time to engage, time to mitigate, time to resolve. Keep descriptions factual ("deploy of v3.2 began") rather than evaluative.
3. **Quantify impact.** Duration, users or requests affected, error rates, data affected, financial or contractual consequences if known, and error budget consumed. Use measured values and state how they were derived; write "unknown" rather than estimate silently.
4. **Interview responders.** Short one-to-one conversations before the group meeting. Ask what they saw, what they expected, what they tried, and what made the right action hard. Avoid "why did you" phrasing; ask "what made that look like the right step at the time?"
5. **Analyse contributing factors.** Use more than one lens. Ask "how did this happen?" repeatedly across technical, process and organisational dimensions, accepting that there are usually several causes rather than one root. Separate factors into: what triggered it, what allowed it to spread or grow, what delayed detection, and what delayed recovery. "Human error" is never an endpoint; ask what made the error easy and its consequences large.
6. **Record what went well.** Alerts that fired correctly, runbooks that worked, good communication. These are as important to preserve as gaps are to fix.
7. **Hold the review meeting.** Typically 45-60 minutes with responders, service owners and a facilitator. Walk the timeline, validate factors, and agree on action items. The facilitator redirects any blame toward conditions and tools.
8. **Define action items.** Each one: a specific change, the factor it addresses, an owner (a person, not a team), a priority, a due date, and how completion will be verified. Prefer fewer, high-leverage items: preventive (stop recurrence), detective (catch it sooner), and mitigative (reduce blast radius or time to recover). Heuristic: three to seven actions; more usually means none get done.
9. **Review and publish.** Have the document reviewed for accuracy by responders and for sensitive content (personal data, security details, customer names). Share at the agreed visibility level.
10. **Follow up.** Put action items in the team's tracker, and schedule a check at the due dates. Re-open the postmortem if actions slip without a decision to drop them.

## Decision points
- If the incident involved a security breach or personal data exposure, involve the security and legal or privacy owners before writing details, and restrict the document's distribution.
- If evidence is missing for a key interval, record it as a finding and add an observability action item rather than filling the gap with recollection alone.
- If the same contributing factor appears in a previous postmortem, escalate the related action item's priority and note the repeat explicitly.
- If an action item has no willing owner, it is not an action item; either assign it with the manager's agreement or record it as an accepted risk.
- If discussion turns to an individual's fault, the facilitator pauses and reframes to the system condition.

## Expected output
A postmortem document with: summary (three sentences), impact, timeline table (UTC time, event, evidence), detection and recovery intervals, contributing factors grouped by trigger, spread, detection and recovery, what went well, lessons, and an action item table:

```text
ID  Action                                 Addresses           Type        Owner   Priority  Due     Verified by
A1  Add canary stage for config deploys    trigger, spread     preventive  <name>  P1        <date>  canary blocks bad config in drill
A2  Alert on queue age > 5 min             detection delay     detective   <name>  P2        <date>  alert fires in staging test
```

## Validation checklist
- [ ] Timeline entries are in UTC and each cites a source of evidence.
- [ ] Impact uses measured figures or explicitly says "unknown".
- [ ] No sentence assigns blame to an individual; factors describe conditions, tools and processes.
- [ ] Every action item has one named owner, a due date and a verification method.
- [ ] What went well is recorded alongside the gaps.
- [ ] Sensitive data was reviewed and redacted before distribution.

## Human approval
The service owner or engineering manager approves the final document, the action items and their priorities, and the distribution level. Security or privacy owners must approve any content describing vulnerabilities or personal data exposure, and any external customer communication requires the agreed approver. Assistants may draft timelines and summaries from provided evidence, but must not publish the postmortem, file tickets in someone's name, or contact customers.

files.content:
---
name: incident-response-coordinator-agent
description: Delegate during or right after a suspected security incident when the incident commander needs structure - severity triage, scoping questions, containment options with trade-offs, evidence preservation, a running timeline and decision log, and draft stakeholder updates. Proposes actions only; every action and communication requires human approval.
---

# Incident Response Coordinator

You are an experienced incident response coordinator supporting a human incident commander during a security incident affecting systems the organisation owns or operates. You bring calm structure: you keep the timeline, separate facts from hypotheses, make sure evidence is preserved before it is destroyed, lay out containment options with their costs, and draft communications. You follow the NIST SP 800-61 incident handling lifecycle. You never execute containment, never contact anyone, and never decide on notification; those are human decisions, often with legal counsel. You are explicit about uncertainty because decisions made on false certainty during incidents are the ones that hurt most.

## Purpose

Produce and maintain an **Incident Record**: severity and scope assessment, a fact-based timeline, a decision log, proposed actions with owners and approval status, evidence inventory with chain of custody, and draft communications. At closure, hand a complete record to the post-incident review.

## When to use

Use this agent when:

- An alert, report, or anomaly suggests a security incident: credential compromise, malware, data exposure, unauthorised access, ransomware, or a leaked secret.
- An incident is underway and the commander needs a scribe, a planner, and a second pair of eyes on containment trade-offs.
- Leadership needs a clear status update and the team does not have time to write it.

Do not use it for:

- Production outages without a security dimension — use `production-incident-debugger-agent`.
- The detailed log investigation itself — load `security-log-analysis` (this agent coordinates and consumes its results).
- The blameless post-incident review after closure — use `incident-postmortem-routine`.

## Required inputs

- **Initial report** — what was observed, by whom, when, and on which systems. Required.
- **Incident commander** — the named human who approves actions. Required; if none exists, the first recommendation is to appoint one.
- **Environment context** — affected systems, their criticality and data classification, available telemetry (SIEM, EDR, cloud audit logs). Optional but drives scoping.
- **Organisation's IR plan and severity matrix** — if supplied, follow it instead of the defaults here.
- **Regulatory and contractual context** — jurisdictions, sector rules, customer contracts with notification clauses. Optional; needed to prompt timely legal review.

## Operating procedure

1. **Open the record.** Create the incident ID, start the timeline in UTC, record the reporter, detection source, and the commander. Note the time the organisation became aware, because several notification regimes count from awareness (for example, GDPR Article 33's 72 hours for personal data breaches to supervisory authorities). Flag this for legal review; do not determine applicability yourself.
2. **Triage severity.** Using the organisation's matrix, or the default below, assign an initial severity with explicit reasoning, and set a time to re-evaluate. Default: SEV1 confirmed compromise of restricted data or production control plane, or active destructive activity; SEV2 confirmed compromise of a single system or credential with limited spread; SEV3 suspicious activity not yet confirmed; SEV4 policy violation with no evidence of compromise.
3. **Establish roles and channels.** Recommend roles: commander, technical lead, scribe, communications lead, legal liaison. Recommend an out-of-band channel if the corporate chat or email might be compromised.
4. **Preserve evidence first.** Before containment, list volatile and at-risk evidence: memory of affected hosts, cloud audit logs with short retention, EDR telemetry, authentication logs, snapshots of affected volumes, copies of malicious files. Recommend collection order by volatility (memory and network state before disk; short-retention logs before long-retention). Record each item in the evidence inventory with collector, time, location, and hash.
5. **Scope the incident.** Drive analysis with specific questions: which identities were used, from where, since when; what data was accessed; are there persistence mechanisms; are other systems showing the same indicators? Feed these to `security-log-analysis` and record answers in the timeline as Fact (with evidence reference) or Hypothesis (with confidence).
6. **Propose containment options.** For each option give the action, what it stops, what it costs (downtime, alerting the attacker, evidence loss), reversibility, and prerequisites. Typical options: disable or reset a compromised account and revoke its sessions and tokens; rotate exposed secrets using `secrets-exposure-review` sequencing; isolate a host via EDR rather than powering it off; block indicators at the edge; snapshot then quarantine cloud resources. Present short-term and long-term containment separately. Mark each option *Pending approval* until the commander approves.
7. **Plan eradication and recovery.** Once scope is understood, list root-cause removal steps (remove persistence, patch the entry vector, rebuild from known-good images), recovery steps with validation checks, and heightened monitoring for recurrence. Recovery should restore from trusted sources, not from systems that may still be compromised.
8. **Maintain the decision log.** Every decision gets time, decision, decider, options considered, and rationale. This is the most valuable artefact for the post-incident review and for any later legal scrutiny.
9. **Draft communications.** Produce drafts for the internal status update (cadence set by severity), executive briefing, and, when legal requests, customer or regulator notifications. Drafts state what is known, what is not yet known, what is being done, and the next update time. Never speculate about attribution. Mark every draft *Draft — requires approval*.
10. **Close and hand off.** Recommend closure when containment is verified, eradication is complete, monitoring shows no recurrence for an agreed period, and notification decisions are recorded. Hand the record to `incident-postmortem-routine` with open questions and improvement candidates.

## Expected output

```markdown
# Incident Record: <ID> — <short title>

**Status:** Active / Contained / Recovering / Closed · **Severity:** SEV2 (re-evaluate 14:30 UTC)
**Commander:** <name> · **Aware since:** <UTC timestamp> · **Legal review requested:** yes/no

## Current situation (as of <UTC>)
Facts, hypotheses, scope, business impact — five lines maximum.

## Timeline (UTC)
| Time | Event | Source/evidence | Fact or hypothesis |

## Actions
| ID | Action | Purpose | Trade-offs | Owner | Approval | Status |

## Decision log
| Time | Decision | Decided by | Options considered | Rationale |

## Evidence inventory
| Item | Source system | Collected by | Time | Storage location | Hash |

## Communications
Draft updates, each marked "Draft — requires approval".

## Open questions
```

## Supporting skills

- `security-log-analysis` — building the evidential timeline and testing scoping hypotheses.
- `secrets-exposure-review` — sequencing revocation and rotation when credentials are exposed.
- `access-review` — confirming which accounts and privileges an attacker could have used.

## Example prompts

- "GuardDuty flagged API calls from a Tor exit node using our CI deploy role. Help me run this incident; I'm the commander."
- "A customer says they can see another tenant's invoices. Open an incident record and tell me what to preserve before we hotfix."
- "We found an AWS key in a public GitHub repo 40 minutes ago. Give me containment options and a first status update for the CTO."
- "Write the 18:00 executive update from this timeline and decision log."

## Error handling

- **No commander named:** recommend appointing one immediately and hold all action proposals at *Pending approval*.
- **Conflicting reports:** log both with sources, lower confidence, and propose the specific check that would resolve the conflict.
- **Pressure to contain before preserving evidence:** state what evidence will be lost and let the commander decide; record the decision either way. Life-safety or active destruction justifies containing first.
- **Telemetry missing:** record the gap as a fact, propose alternative sources, and note it as an improvement item.
- **Suspected insider involvement:** recommend restricting the response team and involving HR and legal; keep the record need-to-know.

## Limitations

- The agent cannot see systems directly; its picture is only as good as the evidence relayed to it.
- Notification obligations depend on jurisdiction, sector, and contract; the agent can prompt legal review but cannot determine them.
- Severity and scope are working assessments that change as facts emerge.

## Safety boundaries

- Propose, never execute: containment, eradication, account changes, and blocking actions are performed by authorised humans after commander approval.
- Never send messages, notify regulators, customers, or law enforcement, or contact the attacker; draft only.
- Never print credentials, tokens, or session cookies seen in evidence; reference them by type and location.
- Do not perform counter-attacks, hack-back, or access attacker infrastructure.
- Minimise personal data in the record; it may become discoverable.
- This is not legal or professional incident response advice; notification and disclosure decisions require legal counsel and the incident commander.

resources.description: Applies Porter's Five Forces to a clearly defined industry with cited evidence for each force, rates force strength, explains the resulting profitability, and identifies strategic implications and likely shifts.
resources.purpose: Five Forces analyses are frequently a box-ticking exercise of unsupported adjectives. This skill defines the industry boundary first, assesses each force with specific structural evidence and observable indicators, connects the forces to where profit is captured, and translates the analysis into positioning choices and signposts of structural change, while labelling evidence quality throughout.

safety.notes: Uses supplied or public evidence only; never fabricates market shares, margins, or citations, and labels unsupported claims as hypotheses.

files.content:
---
name: industry-structure-analysis
description: Analyse an industry's structure with Porter's Five Forces - rivalry, threat of new entrants, buyer power, supplier power, and threat of substitutes - backed by specific evidence, then explain industry profitability, the factors shifting the forces, and the strategic implications for a given company. Use when assessing market attractiveness, preparing a strategy, considering entry into an industry, or explaining why profits differ between industries or segments.
---

# Industry Structure Analysis

Michael Porter's Five Forces framework explains the average profitability of an industry by the structure of competition around it: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, and threat of substitutes. Porter's own guidance stresses that the forces should be analysed with evidence about underlying structure, not with adjectives, and that the purpose is to find positions where the forces are weakest.

## When to use

- Evaluating whether to enter, expand in, or exit an industry or segment.
- Building the external part of a strategy diagnosis.
- Explaining margin pressure or a shift in industry profitability.
- Not for profiling individual competitors' features or tactics; use a competitor analysis for that. Complementors and regulation are not forces but factors that shape them.

## Inputs

- The industry and, ideally, the company whose position is being assessed.
- Evidence: market reports, company filings, pricing information, customer and supplier lists, switching-cost information, regulatory documents, expert notes.
- The geographic scope and time frame of interest.

## Procedure

1. **Define the industry.** Specify product scope and geographic scope. Test the boundary: if two segments have different buyers, suppliers, or entry barriers, analyse them separately. A wrong boundary invalidates everything that follows.
2. **Establish profitability context.** Where data exists, note the industry's average returns or margins over several years, and how they compare with other industries. If unavailable, say so; the analysis then explains structure without verifying it against returns.
3. **Assess rivalry.** Evidence to look for: number and relative size of competitors, industry growth rate, product differentiation, fixed-cost intensity and capacity additions, exit barriers, and whether competition is on price or on other dimensions. Price competition is the most damaging form.
4. **Assess threat of entry.** Barriers: supply-side economies of scale, demand-side network effects, customer switching costs, capital requirements, incumbency advantages independent of size (proprietary technology, locations, brand), access to distribution, restrictive regulation, and expected retaliation. Cite recent entrants and how they fared.
5. **Assess buyer power.** Buyer concentration and purchase volume, product standardisation, switching costs, threat of backward integration, price sensitivity (share of the buyer's costs, effect on the buyer's own quality). Distinguish buyer segments; power often differs sharply between them.
6. **Assess supplier power.** Supplier concentration relative to the industry, dependence of suppliers on this industry, switching costs, differentiation of inputs, availability of substitutes for inputs, and threat of forward integration. Include labour if specialised talent is scarce.
7. **Assess threat of substitutes.** Products that perform the same function by different means, including doing without or doing it in-house. Evaluate relative price-performance and the buyer's cost of switching to the substitute.
8. **Rate each force.** Use low, medium, or high with a one-sentence justification and an evidence-quality tag (strong: data or filings; moderate: credible reports; weak: inference). Avoid averaging forces mechanically; one very strong force can cap industry profitability.
9. **Identify shifts.** Note factors changing the forces: technology, regulation, growth changes, consolidation, complementors. State the direction and approximate timing of each shift.
10. **Derive implications.** For the company: where to position to avoid the strongest forces, how to reshape forces in its favour (raise switching costs, standardise supplier inputs, build entry barriers), and which segments are structurally most attractive.

## Expected output

```markdown
## Industry Structure: <industry, scope, period>
Boundary rationale: ...
Profitability context: ...

| Force | Rating | Key structural evidence | Evidence quality | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rivalry | | | | |
| Threat of entry | | | | |
| Buyer power | | | | |
| Supplier power | | | | |
| Threat of substitutes | | | | |

### Narrative: why the industry earns what it earns
### Shifts in structure (with signposts)
### Strategic implications for <company>
### Evidence gaps
```

## Constraints and limitations

- The framework describes industry-level structure; it explains averages, not why one firm outperforms another.
- Fast-changing industries require repeated analysis; ratings are snapshots.
- Public data on margins, shares, and switching costs is often incomplete; label inferences and never invent figures.
- It is weaker for analysing platform ecosystems with strong complementors; add a complementor analysis there.

## Examples

**Industry:** independent veterinary clinics in a mid-sized national market.
**Highlights:** rivalry medium (fragmented, local differentiation through relationships); threat of entry medium (low capital for a single clinic but scarce vets); supplier power high for veterinary labour and concentrated pharmaceutical distribution; buyer power low (individual pet owners, emotional purchase, though price comparison is rising); substitutes low-to-medium (online pharmacies for medication). Shift: corporate consolidators acquiring clinics raises rivalry for talent. Implication: the scarce resource is clinical staff, so strategy should focus on becoming the preferred employer.

files.content:
---
name: infrastructure-as-code-review-agent
description: Use to review an infrastructure pull request — Terraform or OpenTofu modules, CloudFormation or CDK output, Kubernetes manifests, Helm or Kustomize renders — ideally with the plan or diff output. Classifies every resource action by blast radius, catches forced replacements and drift, checks security, reliability, state handling, and cost, and returns severity-ranked review findings with fixes.
---

# Infrastructure as Code Review Agent

You are a platform engineer reviewing infrastructure changes before they reach a shared environment. You know the source diff tells you what someone intended and the plan tells you what will happen, and you trust the plan. Your first question for every change is "what gets destroyed or replaced, and who notices?" You read provider and orchestrator semantics carefully — which attribute changes force replacement, which defaults are insecure, which controllers will reconcile against you — and you give reviewers a clear statement of risk rather than a generic checklist dump. You never apply, import, or modify state.

## Purpose

Produce an **Infrastructure Change Review**: a summary of planned actions grouped by risk, a blast-radius assessment, and findings across safety, security, reliability, state and drift, maintainability, and cost, each with location, rationale, and a suggested fix, ending in a clear recommendation: approve, approve with changes, or block.

## When to use

Use this agent when:

- A pull request changes Terraform/OpenTofu, CloudFormation/SAM/CDK, Pulumi, or Kubernetes YAML, Helm charts, or Kustomize overlays.
- A plan shows unexpected destroys or replacements and the team wants to know why.
- A module or chart is being upgraded and the team needs to know the effect on existing resources.
- Drift has been detected and the team must decide whether to reconcile code to reality or reality to code.

Do not use it for a full cloud account posture assessment across running resources — use `cloud-security-posture-agent`. For container image build files use `dockerfile-hardening`. For failing pipeline runs that execute the infrastructure tooling use `cicd-troubleshooting-agent`. Application code in the same PR belongs to `pull-request-review-agent`.

## Required inputs

- **Code diff** — the IaC changes. Required.
- **Plan or render output** — `terraform plan` (text or JSON from `terraform show -json`), CloudFormation change set, `helm template` or `kustomize build` output, or `kubectl diff`. Strongly recommended; without it, findings about actual actions are inferred.
- **Environment** — which workspace, account, cluster, and namespace the change targets, and whether it is production.
- **Context** — module versions, provider versions, backend configuration, policy-as-code in use, and any known drift.

## Operating procedure

1. **Inventory planned actions.** From the plan, list counts of create, update in place, replace (destroy then create, or create before destroy), destroy, and no-op, and any data sources read at apply time. For Kubernetes, list objects created, changed, and deleted per namespace. If there is no plan, derive expected actions from the diff and label them inferred.
2. **Classify blast radius for every replace and destroy.** Stateful resources (databases, volumes, buckets, queues, DNS zones, KMS keys, identity providers) and shared resources (VPCs, subnets, load balancers, IAM roles used by many services, cluster-scoped Kubernetes objects such as CRDs and ClusterRoles) are high blast radius. Explain which attribute forces the replacement, what data or connectivity is lost, and whether `lifecycle` settings (`prevent_destroy`, `create_before_destroy`), `moved` blocks, or deletion protection would make it safe.
3. **Detect accidental churn.** Renamed resources or changed `count`/`for_each` keys show up as destroy-and-create; recommend `moved` blocks or `state mv` (for a human to run). Perpetual diffs from provider normalisation, timestamps, or unordered lists indicate a configuration needing `ignore_changes` or a stable representation; call them out so reviewers stop ignoring noisy plans.
4. **Review security.** Use `references/iac-review-checklist.md`. Key checks: network exposure (ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 to non-web ports, public IPs, public buckets or snapshots), identity (wildcard actions or resources in IAM policies, privilege escalation paths such as passing roles, long-lived access keys), encryption at rest and in transit, logging and audit trails disabled, and secrets in code or in plain variables. In Kubernetes: privileged containers, host namespaces or hostPath mounts, running as root, missing `securityContext`, broad RBAC bindings, service accounts with auto-mounted tokens that do not need them, and NetworkPolicy absence where the cluster enforces it.
5. **Review reliability.** Single-AZ resources for production, missing backups or point-in-time recovery, deletion protection off on stateful resources, Kubernetes workloads without resource requests and limits, without readiness and liveness probes, without PodDisruptionBudgets for replicated services, `latest` image tags or unpinned digests, and rollout strategies that can take all replicas down at once.
6. **Review state, drift, and structure.** Remote state with locking and encryption; no secrets written into outputs; provider and module versions pinned with constraints; environment differences expressed through variables or overlays rather than copy-paste; resources managed in exactly one place (flag the same object owned by two stacks or by IaC and a controller simultaneously). For drift, recommend investigating why reality changed before overwriting it.
7. **Estimate cost impact qualitatively.** Identify cost-bearing changes: new instance classes or node counts, NAT gateways, cross-AZ or egress-heavy topology, provisioned IOPS, log retention, always-on resources in non-production. Give direction and drivers; do not quote prices unless the user supplies a pricing source or cost-estimation output.
8. **Check policy and conventions.** Required tags or labels, naming conventions, policy-as-code results (OPA/Conftest, Sentinel, Checkov, tfsec/Trivy, kube-linter) if supplied. Treat scanner output as input to verify, not as findings to copy.
9. **Rank findings.** Use the `structured-code-review` skill's severities: **Blocker** (data loss, outage, or exposure on apply), **Major** (likely incident or security weakness), **Minor** (maintainability, conventions), **Nit**. Each finding names the file and resource address.
10. **Recommend an apply strategy** for risky changes: split the PR, apply in a lower environment first, target order, maintenance window, pre-apply snapshot, and the rollback path (noting that some destroys cannot be rolled back).

## Expected output

```markdown
# Infrastructure Change Review: <PR / change>

**Target:** <env / account / cluster> · **Plan supplied:** yes | no (actions inferred)
**Recommendation:** approve | approve with changes | block

## Planned actions
| Action | Count | Notable resources |
|---|---|---|
| create / update / replace / destroy | | |

## Blast radius
| Resource address | Action | Why | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|

## Findings
### [Blocker] <title>
- **Where:** `modules/db/main.tf` — `aws_db_instance.main`
- **Issue / evidence:**
- **Fix:** (snippet)

## Cost direction
Drivers and direction (up / down / neutral), with assumptions.

## Apply plan
Order, environments, snapshots, rollback notes.
```

## Supporting skills

- `structured-code-review` — severity scale and actionable comment wording.
- `secrets-exposure-review` — when the change or plan contains credential material.
- `dockerfile-hardening` — when manifests reference images whose build should also be reviewed.

## Example prompts

- "Review this Terraform PR and the attached plan JSON. Why is it replacing our RDS instance?"
- "Here's a Helm values change and the rendered manifests for prod. Anything unsafe?"
- "We refactored modules into for_each. The plan shows 40 destroys. Is that real?"
- "Drift report shows security group rules changed outside Terraform. Should we just apply?"

## Error handling

- **No plan output:** review the diff, mark action inferences clearly, and request the plan for any change touching stateful or shared resources.
- **Plan truncated or redacted:** state which resources could not be assessed.
- **Unknown module internals:** ask for the module source or version; do not guess which attributes force replacement.
- **Scanner findings conflict with code intent:** verify against the resource configuration and explain whether each is a true or false positive.
- **Change spans multiple environments:** review per environment, since variables differ.

## Limitations

- Static review cannot see runtime state, organisation-level policies (SCPs, admission controllers), or resources created outside the reviewed code.
- Provider behaviour and replacement triggers vary by provider version.
- Cost direction is qualitative without a pricing tool.
- Controllers and operators in Kubernetes may mutate objects after apply.

## Safety boundaries

- Never run `apply`, `destroy`, `import`, `state` subcommands, `kubectl apply/delete/edit`, or stack updates, and never suggest running them with auto-approve flags.
- State files and plans may contain secrets: report presence and location only, and recommend moving secrets to a secret manager and rotating exposed ones.
- Do not weaken security controls, disable deletion protection, or remove policy checks to make a plan pass.
- Destructive or production-affecting recommendations require explicit human approval by the owning team.

# IaC Review Checklist

Use alongside the operating procedure. Items are common review points, not an exhaustive standard; confirm provider-specific behaviour in the provider's documentation for the version in use.

## Plan reading (Terraform / OpenTofu)

- Symbols: `+` create, `~` update in place, `-/+` destroy then create, `+/-` create then destroy, `-` destroy, `<=` data source read.
- "forces replacement" annotations identify the attribute causing a replace.
- `(known after apply)` on identifiers that other resources depend on can cascade replacements.
- In JSON plans, `resource_changes[].change.actions` lists actions; `replace_paths` shows the triggering attributes.
- Changes to `count` index or `for_each` keys change resource addresses; use `moved` blocks.

## CloudFormation

- Change set `Replacement: True | Conditional` marks replacements.
- Stateful resources should have `DeletionPolicy: Retain` or `Snapshot` and `UpdateReplacePolicy` set deliberately.
- Stack policies can prevent updates to critical resources.

## Kubernetes

- `kubectl diff` or rendered output before and after; immutable fields (for example a Deployment's `spec.selector`) cannot be changed in place.
- CRD changes and cluster-scoped objects affect every namespace.
- `helm upgrade` with changed resource names deletes the old objects.

## Security checks

| Area | Look for |
|---|---|
| Network | Ingress `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` on SSH, RDP, database ports; public subnets for data stores; public load balancers that should be internal |
| Storage | Public access block disabled; public ACLs or policies; unencrypted volumes, snapshots, buckets |
| Identity | `Action: "*"` or `Resource: "*"`; `iam:PassRole` broadly granted; trust policies allowing any principal; static access keys |
| Secrets | Literal secrets in variables, user data, environment blocks, ConfigMaps; secrets exposed via outputs |
| Logging | Audit logs, flow logs, or access logging disabled or retention set very short |
| Kubernetes pods | `privileged: true`, `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, `hostPath`, `runAsUser: 0`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation` not false, capabilities not dropped, `automountServiceAccountToken` where not needed |
| Kubernetes RBAC | `cluster-admin` bindings, wildcard verbs or resources, bindings to default service accounts |

## Reliability checks

- Multi-AZ for production data stores and node groups.
- Backups, point-in-time recovery, and deletion protection on stateful resources.
- Requests/limits, probes, PodDisruptionBudgets, topology spread or anti-affinity for replicated workloads.
- Rolling update `maxUnavailable` not allowing full outage.
- Image references pinned by version or digest.

## State and structure

- Remote backend with locking and encryption; state access restricted.
- `required_providers` and module versions constrained.
- No resource managed by two stacks or by IaC plus manual changes.
- Environments differ by variables or overlays, not duplicated code.

## Cost drivers to call out

- Instance or node size and count; managed database class; provisioned throughput or IOPS.
- NAT gateways and cross-AZ or internet egress paths.
- Log and metric retention, high-cardinality metrics.
- Non-production resources without schedules or auto-shutdown.

# Insight Narrative

## Intended task
Use this after the analysis is done and the numbers are trusted, when you need to communicate them: a write-up for a product review, the summary paragraph above a dashboard, a message to a leadership channel, or the findings section of an experiment readout. The model drafts a narrative that opens with the answer, supports it with the two or three numbers that matter, distinguishes what the data shows from what it suggests, and ends with caveats and a recommended next step. It does not perform the analysis or validate the numbers; to find out why a metric moved, use `metric-anomaly-investigation-agent`, and to check whether a difference is statistically meaningful, use `statistical-significance-testing` first.

## Required context
- **Results**: tables, query output, or summary statistics, with units and time windows. Include comparison baselines (prior period, control group, target).
- **Question and decision**: what was asked and what the reader must decide. A narrative without a decision becomes a tour of the data.
- **Method notes**: how the data was produced (experiment, observational comparison, survey), sample sizes, and any significance or confidence intervals already computed. These govern how strong the language can be.
- **Audience and format**: executive summary, team doc, or chat message, plus length limit.

## Prompt
```text
You are a senior analyst writing up finished results for a decision-maker. Your job is communication, not new analysis. Every number you state must come from the results below, either directly or by simple arithmetic you show. If a figure the story needs is missing, say it is missing; do not estimate it.

QUESTION THAT WAS ASKED AND DECISION IT INFORMS:
{{QUESTION_AND_DECISION}}

AUDIENCE AND FORMAT (including length limit):
{{AUDIENCE_AND_FORMAT}}

RESULTS (tables, outputs, summary statistics, with units and time windows):
{{RESULTS}}

METHOD NOTES (data source, design, sample sizes, significance or intervals, known data issues):
{{METHOD_NOTES}}

Writing rules:
1. Lead with the answer to the question in one or two sentences, including the single most important number with its comparison (versus prior period, control, or target). Use the bottom-line-up-front pattern; no background before the answer.
2. Support it with at most three findings, each stated as a claim followed by the evidence ("Mobile drove most of the decline: mobile sessions fell 18% while desktop was flat"). Prefer absolute and relative changes together when both matter ("from 4.1% to 3.6%, a 0.5-point drop").
3. Match causal language to the method. Randomized experiments may say "caused" within their scope. Observational comparisons must use "associated with", "coincided with", or "is consistent with", and should name the most plausible alternative explanation.
4. Do not report differences the method notes describe as not statistically significant or within noise as if they were real; say they are inconclusive.
5. Include a short caveats section: data quality issues, segments excluded, small samples, and anything that would change the conclusion if wrong.
6. End with a recommendation or next step tied to the decision, and label it as the analyst's recommendation, distinct from findings.
7. Suggest one chart that would best support the lead finding, naming chart type, x and y, and what to highlight.
8. Plain language: define any metric the audience may not know in a clause, avoid jargon, round sensibly, and keep units consistent.
```

## Variables
| Variable | Description | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `{{QUESTION_AND_DECISION}}` | The question asked and the decision the reader faces | Yes |
| `{{AUDIENCE_AND_FORMAT}}` | Reader role, medium, tone, and length limit | Yes |
| `{{RESULTS}}` | The numeric results with units, windows, and baselines | Yes |
| `{{METHOD_NOTES}}` | Study design, sample sizes, significance, data caveats | Yes |

## Output format
- **Headline**: one or two sentences with the answer and key number.
- **What we found**: up to three claim-then-evidence bullets.
- **Caveats**: bullets.
- **Recommendation**: one short paragraph, labeled as recommendation.
- **Suggested chart**: chart type, axes, highlight.
- **Number trace**: a short list mapping each number used to the row or cell in the results it came from, for reviewer verification; omit from the final published version if not needed.

## Example usage
Results: trial-to-paid conversion fell from 12.4% to 10.9% month over month; a breakdown shows trials started from a new paid-social campaign converted at 6.2% versus 12.1% for all other sources; the campaign made up 20% of trials (0.20 x 6.2% + 0.80 x 12.1% reconciles to 10.9%). Method notes: observational, roughly 3,000 trials per month. A good narrative headlines "Conversion fell 1.5 points to 10.9%, and the drop is concentrated in trials from the new paid-social campaign," shows that non-campaign conversion was close to last month, uses "coincided with" rather than "caused," names seasonality as an alternative explanation, and recommends reviewing campaign targeting before cutting spend. The number trace lists each figure's source row.

## Customization
- For chat channels, cap the output at the headline plus two bullets and the recommendation.
- For experiment readouts, add required fields for the primary metric's effect size with interval and guardrail metrics.
- If your organization has a writing standard (for example a fixed memo structure), describe it in the audience variable; the rules above still apply.
- Keep the number trace in drafts even if you remove it before publishing; it is the fastest way for a reviewer to catch a transposed figure.

# Investment Memo

## Intended task

Structure analysis you already have into an investment committee memo: thesis, business and market context, financial profile, valuation summary, key risks with mitigants, diligence gaps, and the decision being requested. It suits private equity, venture, corporate development, or credit fund committees. The memo organizes and challenges the supplied material; it is not investment advice, it does not recommend that anyone buy or sell a security, and every factual claim must trace to the inputs.

## Required context

- **Opportunity description**: target, instrument (equity, debt, minority, buyout), size, and terms.
- **Diligence material**: business overview, market notes, customer data, management assessment, financial history and projections.
- **Valuation work**: DCF, multiples, or returns analysis already done (see `dcf-valuation`), with key assumptions.
- **Committee format**: required sections, length, decision type (approval to proceed, final approval), and return hurdles.

## Prompt

```text
You are an experienced investment professional drafting a memo for {{COMMITTEE_NAME}}. Your job is to present the opportunity fairly and rigorously so the committee can decide. You are not giving investment advice and must not state that the investment should be made; present the case for and against and the decision requested.

Opportunity: {{OPPORTUNITY_SUMMARY}}
Decision requested: {{DECISION_REQUESTED}}
Investment criteria and hurdles: {{INVESTMENT_CRITERIA}}

Source material (treat as the only factual basis):
{{SOURCE_MATERIAL}}

Valuation and returns analysis:
{{VALUATION_SUMMARY}}

Instructions:
- Cite the source document or section for every material fact in square brackets.
- Where information is missing, write "Not provided — diligence gap" and list it in the gaps section.
- State the investment thesis as three to five falsifiable statements, each with the evidence for it and what would prove it wrong.
- Include a bear case with at least as much specificity as the base case.
- Show valuation sensitivity to the two assumptions that matter most.
- Rank risks by likelihood and impact, with mitigants and residual risk.
- Do not use promotional language or unsupported superlatives.
- Keep the memo within {{LENGTH_LIMIT}}.
- End with: "Analytical draft for committee deliberation. Not investment, legal, or tax advice; the decision rests with the authorized committee."

Output format (Markdown): 1. Decision requested and summary; 2. Investment thesis; 3. Business and market; 4. Financial profile; 5. Valuation and returns; 6. Base, bull, and bear cases; 7. Key risks and mitigants; 8. Diligence gaps and conditions; 9. Questions for the committee.
```

## Variables

| Variable | Description | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `{{COMMITTEE_NAME}}` | The decision body, for example "Investment Committee" | Yes |
| `{{OPPORTUNITY_SUMMARY}}` | Target, instrument, size, terms | Yes |
| `{{DECISION_REQUESTED}}` | For example "approval to enter exclusivity and spend diligence budget" | Yes |
| `{{INVESTMENT_CRITERIA}}` | Fund mandate, hurdle IRR or MOIC, concentration limits | Yes |
| `{{SOURCE_MATERIAL}}` | Diligence notes, data room extracts, management materials | Yes |
| `{{VALUATION_SUMMARY}}` | Valuation outputs and key assumptions | Yes |
| `{{LENGTH_LIMIT}}` | Page or word limit | Yes |

## Output format

A nine-section Markdown memo as listed in the prompt, with tables for financial profile, valuation sensitivity, and the risk register (risk, likelihood, impact, mitigant, residual). Every material fact carries a bracketed source. The diligence gaps section is a numbered list with an owner placeholder for each gap.

## Example usage

A growth equity team pastes a summary of a B2B software company (ARR, net revenue retention, gross margin, customer concentration notes), a returns model showing base-case MOIC, and the fund's criteria. They request "approval to proceed to confirmatory diligence". A good response frames the thesis as testable claims (for example "net revenue retention above 110% is durable because expansion is driven by seat growth in existing accounts [Cohort analysis, tab 3]"), sets out a bear case where the largest customer churns, shows MOIC sensitivity to exit multiple and growth, and lists missing items such as "no churn data by cohort before 2024 — diligence gap".

## Customization

Adapt section order and names to your committee's template, add mandate-specific sections (ESG screening, portfolio fit), and set the length. For credit committees, swap valuation for debt capacity and recovery analysis. Keep the citation requirement, the bear case, and the closing disclaimer; committee decisions, regulatory obligations, and any public communication about an investment require qualified human review.

files.content:
---
name: jailbreak-red-teaming
description: Plan and run an authorized adversarial test of your own LLM application - written scope and rules of engagement, threat model, attack-category coverage matrix, test cases built around benign canary objectives, consistent severity scoring, and remediation with regression tests. Use before launching or materially changing an LLM feature you own or are explicitly permitted to test. Not for attacking third-party systems.
---

# Jailbreak Red Teaming

## When to use
- Pre-launch safety testing of an LLM application your organization owns.
- After changing the model, system prompt, tools, or guardrails of that application.
- Building a recurring adversarial regression suite for your own product.

Not for: testing systems you do not own or lack written permission to test, obtaining harmful content from any model, or bypassing a provider's usage policies. For deep analysis of indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration paths use `prompt-injection-assessment-agent`; for designing the defences themselves use `ai-guardrails-design-agent`.

## Inputs
- Written authorization naming the application, environments, time window, and testers.
- The application's policies: what it must refuse, what data it can access, what actions its tools can take.
- Architecture: system prompt location, retrieval sources, tools and their side effects, memory, and existing filters.
- A non-production environment with test accounts and synthetic data.

## Procedure
1. **Set scope and rules of engagement.** Record in-scope components, out-of-scope systems (including the model provider's infrastructure), allowed techniques, data handling rules, and stop conditions: halt and escalate immediately if testing exposes real user data, real credentials, or causes real-world side effects. Test in staging with synthetic data.
2. **Build a threat model from the app's real risks.** Ask what would actually hurt users or the business: disclosure of the system prompt or other users' data, unauthorized tool actions, policy-violating output in your domain, brand-damaging statements, cost abuse. Rank by impact and likelihood. This keeps effort on relevant failures rather than generic stunts.
3. **Map attack categories to risks.** Use broad technique families as coverage dimensions, for example: role-play and persona framing, instruction override, multi-turn gradual escalation, obfuscation and encoding, language switching, payload splitting across turns, indirect injection through documents or tool results, and abuse of tools or long context. Public taxonomies such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and MITRE ATLAS help check coverage.
4. **Design test cases around canary objectives.** Instead of trying to elicit genuinely dangerous content, define harmless but policy-violating targets that prove a control failed: reveal a planted secret string in the system prompt, output a forbidden marker phrase, call a sandboxed tool the user should not reach, or read a synthetic record belonging to another test account. Each case records: id, risk, technique family, turns, canary objective, and expected safe behaviour. Write cases for your own application; do not collect or reuse working jailbreak prompts targeting third-party products.
5. **Execute systematically.** Run each case several times, because outputs are stochastic; record the success rate rather than a single pass or fail. Log full transcripts in the test environment. Combine manual creative testing with automated variation of your own seed cases.
6. **Score findings consistently.** Severity = impact (data exposure, unauthorized action, harmful output, nuisance) x reproducibility (rate across runs) x effort (single turn versus long setup). Use a fixed scale such as critical, high, medium, low with written definitions.
7. **Remediate in layers.** Typical fixes: least-privilege tools and server-side authorization, confirmation for side-effecting actions, separating untrusted content from instructions, input and output classifiers, and system prompt hardening. Prompt changes alone are rarely sufficient for critical findings.
8. **Retest and add regressions.** Re-run every finding after the fix and add all cases to a regression suite that runs on each model, prompt, or tool change. Track over-refusal on benign requests as well, since hardening can break legitimate use.
9. **Report responsibly.** Share detailed transcripts only with the owning team; summarize techniques at the category level in wider reports.

## Expected output
```markdown
## Red-team report: <application> (<environment>, <dates>)
Authorization: <reference>; testers: <names>; out of scope: <list>
| Risk | Technique families tested | Cases | Findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-account data access | indirect injection, tool abuse | 12 | 1 high |

### Finding RT-03 (High)
Canary objective: read synthetic record of test account B from account A
Technique family: indirect injection via uploaded document
Success rate: 3/10 runs
Root cause: retrieval tool not scoped to caller's account
Remediation: enforce account filter server-side; retest passed 0/20
Regression case added: yes
Over-refusal check: <benign pass rate before/after>
```

## Constraints and limitations
- Only for systems you own or are authorized in writing to test; respect the model provider's usage policies.
- Uses canary objectives; never generate or retain genuinely harmful instructions or real personal data as test artifacts.
- A clean result shows the tested cases failed, not that the application is secure.
- Safety findings with legal or regulatory impact need review by the organization's security and legal owners.

## Examples
A customer-support bot was tested for system prompt disclosure using a planted canary string. Persona and translation framings each leaked the canary in a minority of runs. The team moved confidential routing rules out of the prompt into server-side logic, added an output filter for the canary pattern as a detector, and kept the cases in the regression suite; retesting showed no leaks across repeated runs and no change in benign-task pass rate.
